summary: Motion Assist to save the day.
body: Motion sickness is not a fun thing to deal with. While I don’t personally struggle with it, I’ve known people who do, and it seems like it can be pretty unbearable at times. title: These unofficial Sony apps let you ditch your phone to control your headphones
summary: Tired of Sony’s Sound Connect app? These PC tools put headphone controls on your desktop.
body: TL;DR Getting the most out of Sony headphones and earbuds means relying on the company’s phone app to adjust audio settings. Now some open source projects attempt to unofficially bring that same level of control to your PC. They let you control ANC, tweak your equalizer, and adjust many more audio options. Being able to control devices through apps on our phones is a bit of a double-edged sword. Sure, apps can open up tons of new features, and being able to configure devices remotely lets manufactures simplify hardware designs. But the flip side there is that making even basic changes means that we need our phone — and that’s not always handy. They protect everything from our emails and social media accounts to banking apps and personal photos, so the last thing you want is to accidentally leave them exposed. Unfortunately, that can become a concern when you decide to switch password managers. Right now, you may have to export your entire vault as a file, save it to your device, and then import it into your new password manager . Fitness trackers have happily told us how much we moved, how poorly we slept, and how fast our hearts beat, then largely left us to connect the dots. At its big iPhone launch event , Apple finally brought that idea to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with a new feature called Readiness. Readiness combines recent activity and vitals, including sleep duration, blood oxygen, HRV, respiratory rate, and resting heart rate, into a score from zero to ten. Apple then translates that number into one of four refreshingly direct recommendations: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. Apple has added visible and audible privacy safeguards, but a watch that can recall what was just said may still feel unsettling. Wouldn’t it be a little creepy if I told you the watch on your wrist could rewind the last 15 seconds of your life? Well, that’s essentially what Apple’s new Live Rewind feature can do. Apple announced the feature alongside the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 today, and despite the slightly creepy premise, it’s easy to imagine situations where it could be genuinely useful. Over the generations we’ve already seen, manufacturers have been making foldable phones more and more robust — what were once incredibly finnicky, fragile designs, have reached something approaching the reliability we’re used to from regular, non-foldable models.
